{{Short description|Artificial boundary condition for outgoing waves}}
In [[numerical analysis]] of [[wave equation|wave]] problems, '''absorbing boundary conditions''', '''non-reflecting boundary conditions'''<ref name="givoli1991"/> or '''transmitting boundaries'''<ref name="kausel1988"/> are artificial [[Boundary value problem|boundary conditions]] applied at the edges of a finite computational domain to allow outgoing [[wave]]s to pass out of the grid without generating reflections. 

In many physical problems, such as [[acoustics]], [[electromagnetics]], and [[fluid dynamics]], waves naturally propagate into an infinite or semi-infinite space. However, numerical methods like [[finite difference method|finite difference]] or [[finite element method]]s require a finite, truncated grid to remain computationally feasible. Without an effective absorbing boundary condition, waves reaching the artificial boundary of the simulation would reflect back into the interior, causing non-physical interference and spurious echoes that contaminate the results.

==Background and history==
A perfect absorbing boundary condition would be [[Nonlocal operator|nonlocal]], meaning that the behavior at one point on the boundary depends on the history of the wave field at all other points on the boundary. While mathematically exact, these non-local conditions are often too computationally expensive for large-scale simulations. Consequently, most practical absorbing boundary conditions utilize local approximations based on the differential properties of the wave field.<ref name="givoli1991"/><ref name="kausel1988"/> Beyond purely mathematical boundary operators, many implementations utilize material absorbers such as the [[perfectly matched layer]], which simulate an artificial physical region where waves are gradually attenuated through absorptive properties before they reach the simulation's edge.<ref name="teixeira2000"/><ref name="grote2000"/><ref name="hu2004"/> 

Early absorbing boundary conditions, adopted until the 1970s, were based on the application of [[Sommerfeld radiation condition]]; these are denoted as the zeroth-order boundary conditions. From the late 1970s to the mid-1980s, low-order absorbing boundary conditions, such as Bayliss–Turkel and [[Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary condition]]s were introduced.<ref name="givoli2004"/> The 1990s saw the introduction of perfectly matched layers,<ref name="berenger1994"/> as well as higher-order local boundary conditions.<ref name="givoli2004"/>

==List of absorbing boundary conditions==
* Ang–Newmark boundary condition<ref name="kausel1988"/>
* Bayliss–Turkel radiation boundary condition<ref name="bayliss1980"/>
* Complementary operator method<ref name="ramahi1997"/>
* Grote–Keller nonreflecting boundary condition<ref name="grote1995"/>
* Higdon's absorbing boundary condition<ref name="higdon"/>
* [[Engquist–Majda absorbing boundary condition]]<ref name="engquist1977"/>
** Generalized Trefethen–Halpern absorbing boundary condition<ref name="trefethen1986"/>
** Mur absorbing boundary condition<ref name="mur1981"/>
* Liao–Wong absorbing boundary condition<ref name="liao1984"/>
* Lysmer–Kuhlemeyer boundary condition<ref name="lysmer1969"/>
* [[Perfectly matched layer]]<ref name="berenger1994"/>
